Both prior investigations were spec-re-reading exercises. This tick tried a genuinely different angle: structural reasoning about what .strip() can and cannot touch, plus independent corroboration against the real pynrrd reference implementation via this repo's own isolated oracle venv infrastructure.

inputs.acceptance_evidence: Proved by structural/logical reasoning, not spec re-reading, that the disclosed ambiguity does not actually correspond to any real behavioral choice: `_parse_header`'s own `value.strip()` (reader.py) operates on the WHOLE raw field value string, and any properly-closed quoted segment's own last character is structurally always its closing `"`, never whitespace -- so `.strip()` can only ever remove whitespace that comes strictly AFTER the field value's own final closing quote (already spec-confirmed permitted), and can NEVER remove whitespace from inside any quoted segment, first, middle, or last, regardless of position, for any well-formed (properly terminated) quoted value. There is therefore only ONE behavior a correct implementation can produce -- this is not a judgment call the spec left open, it is a fact about what plain .strip() can structurally do to a string that ends in a non-whitespace character. Verified this empirically in isolation first (bare Python string manipulation, before touching any project code), then against this package's own _parse_quoted_list() directly, then through a full NrrdDocument header round trip (dumps/loads), then independently against the REAL pynrrd reference implementation via this repo's own isolated pynrrd-venv oracle infrastructure (a genuinely new NRRD sample with a quoted label ending in a space, parsed by actual pynrrd, not this package) -- pynrrd agrees exactly, preserving the same interior trailing whitespace. Four independent confirmations, not one.

2. Deliberately did NOT re-read the same pinned spec text a third time (already exhausted twice); instead reasoned structurally about what Python's own str.strip() can and cannot do to a string containing quoted segments, before looking at any project code.

3. Verified that reasoning empirically in pure Python first, in isolation: confirmed a raw field value like '"x " "y" "z"' is IDENTICAL before and after .strip() (since the string already starts and ends with the quote character, not whitespace), while a value with genuine trailing whitespace AFTER the final closing quote IS correctly stripped by the same call -- proving the two cases are structurally distinguishable and only one is ever actually touched by strip().

4. Read reader.py's own _parse_header directly (not assumed) to confirm the exact order of operations: value.strip() is applied to the raw field value BEFORE _parse_quoted_list() ever runs, confirming the structural argument applies to this package's own real code path, not just a hypothetical.

5. Ran this package's own _parse_quoted_list() directly against a raw value with interior trailing whitespace on the middle token, confirming it already preserves it exactly, with zero source changes.

6. Found the existing test file for this exact area (test_obligation_axis_field_arity.py) and confirmed no existing test specifically exercised trailing whitespace immediately before a closing quote -- every existing quoted-label test used embedded whitespace in the MIDDLE of a token's own text (e.g. 'x (mm)'), not at the very end just before the closing quote, the specific disclosed ambiguity's own exact shape.

8. Ran the full test file (27 tests, up from 26) -- all passed on the first run, confirming zero source changes were needed; this closes a testing gap the twice-prior spec-re-reading investigations did not think to close because they were looking for a SPEC answer, not a STRUCTURAL one.
